newsitem.title: USA: Who starts a new business -- and how long should it take?
newsitem.headline: Who starts a new business -- and how long should it take?

text.p: Most of us probably have several acquaintances who are always talking about going into business on their own but just never seem to get it started.
They read business magazines and books, take in all the business shows on radio and television, and their collections of business publications could fill a small library.
Then there are others who seem to make it a way of life -- they open businesses, grow them, sell them and start anew.

A survey released in late August by the National Federation of Independent Businesses found that nearly 4.5 million people started new businesses in this country last year. Many of them were repeaters -- people who started one business, closed it and started another.

About one in 10 of the households involved with new businesses had people involved with more than one venture over a six-month period. In some cases, people may have had one business, determined quickly that it wasn't going anywhere, and transferred the assets to another.
"There were clearly some households in this country that seem to do this almost as a way of life," said William Dennis, senior researcher at the NFIB's Education Foundation, in Washington.

However, of the start-ups, about one in four were actually part-time businesses, where the owners spent less than 40 hours a week working in it, worked out of their homes, had no employees and did not even have a business phone number.
But at least they were actually doing something toward reaching their goals of self-employment.

"When a business starts, there is no sequence of events or combination of actions that determines that you're in business," said Dennis. "You can ask 'Did you borrow money? Did you get a location? Did you have sales?' But you can't really come up with a description of when a business starts.
"Essentially, if they feel they have a situation where they think they're in business, they are."

Paul Reynolds, professor of entrepreneurial studies at Babson College in Wellesley, Mass., says the determination of whether or not one is in business is much simpler -- if you have sales and revenue, you're in business.
"If you're not selling something, you're not in business," he said. "You can spend a lot of money before you actually have sales, but if you don't have sales, you're not in business."
Reynolds said that in his surveys of enterepreneurs, "Among the things we did was to ask them about 20 things they did to start a business. We find that no pattern emerges."

Although the commonly recommended method is to develop a thorough business plan before spending a cent on equipment or supplies, Reynolds said that among a sample of about 100 entrepreneurs, about 20 percent said it was only after the business was going that they sat down and thought about it.

One study on which Reynolds worked looked at the sequence of events around the efforts by 71 "nascent entrepreneurs" to start new businesses. They were defined as "individuals who were identified as taking steps to found a new business but who had not yet succeeded in making the transition to new business ownership" -- some surely similar to those aforementioned acquaintances of ours.

The study found that those who actually ended up starting businesses were more aggressive in making their businesses real. They looked for facilities and equipment, sought and got financial support, formed a legal entity, organised a team and devoted themselves full-time to the business.
The average time a firm was in the emerging process was one year, although 20 percent were up and running within one month and 90 percent completed the process within three years.

In contrast, many of the would-be entrepreneurs who did not actually get their businesses going after six months of effort seemed to get bogged down in their preparations. "These entrepreneurs focused on saving money to invest in the business, preparing a business plan and organising a start-up team," said Reynolds.
The entrepreneurs who gave up and were no longer actively trying to establish a business appeared to be somewhat less aggressive than those who started operations.
Some of those who gave up actually did so after developing models or prototypes for their businesses.

"These entrepreneurs discovered that their initial idea for their businesses would not lead to success," Reynolds and his colleagues said. "This group of individuals might be seen as either having the wisdom to test their ideas out before jumping into something that might lead to failure, or lacking the flexibility to find more creative ways to solve the problems they were confronted with."

Then there was a third group that was still trying to launch after a lengthy gestation period. They may well have been involved in trying to develop businesses that inherently required more time and effort, such as highly technological enterprises.
But like our acquaintances, they may also just fall in the category of being all talk and little action.
